title: Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

questions.title: Defining Characteristics of a Pure Monopoly
questions.prompt_template: Which set of market characteristics defines a pure monopoly?

hints.text: Consider the number of sellers, the availability of substitutes, and the ease of entry into the industry.
A pure monopoly stands at the opposite extreme from perfect competition, where many firms sell standardized goods with free entry.

options_template.text: A single seller offering a unique product with no close substitutes, protected by insurmountable barriers to entry.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A pure monopoly consists of one seller producing a unique good without close substitutes, shielded from rival entry by high barriers.

options_template.text: A few dominant sellers offering differentiated products with low barriers to long-run entry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market Structure Confusion): A few interdependent sellers with differentiated goods describes an oligopoly, and low entry barriers would erode long-run market power.

options_template.text: A single seller offering a standardized commodity in a market with free entry and exit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Entry-Barrier Omission): Without barriers to entry, positive economic profits quickly attract competing firms and eliminate the single-seller status.

options_template.text: Many small sellers offering identical products who collectively face a horizontal market demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect Competition Inversion): Many small price-taking sellers of identical goods define perfect competition—and even there, the market demand curve slopes downward while each individual firm's demand is horizontal.

questions.title: Identifying Sources of Barriers to Entry
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following is NOT one of the four primary sources of barriers to entry that sustain a monopoly?

hints.text: Recall the four textbook sources of barriers: resource control, legal protections, network effects, and economies of scale.
Ask which option actually describes a force that undermines or contradicts monopoly power rather than protecting it.

options_template.text: Exclusive ownership or control of a key resource required for production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misclassified Barrier): Exclusive control of an essential input is a classic structural barrier to entry because rivals cannot obtain the input needed to compete.

options_template.text: Government-created legal protections such as patents, copyrights, and exclusive public franchises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misclassified Barrier): Patents, copyrights, and public franchises are legal monopolies explicitly created by government policy to restrict entry.

options_template.text: The availability of numerous close substitutes produced at constant returns to scale.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Numerous close substitutes and constant returns to scale weaken market power and allow easy entry rather than acting as a barrier to entry.

options_template.text: Strong network effects that make a platform more valuable as more users join.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misclassified Barrier): Network effects create a powerful barrier to entry because smaller newcomers struggle to attract users away from an established network.

questions.title: Cost Structure of a Natural Monopoly
questions.prompt_template: What cost condition creates a natural monopoly in industries such as municipal water mains or regional electric distribution grids?

hints.text: Focus on how Long-Run Average Total Cost (LRATC) behaves across the relevant range of market demand.
In a natural monopoly, massive fixed infrastructure costs make one large provider cheaper per unit than two or more smaller providers.

options_template.text: Long-Run Average Total Cost rises steeply at low output levels due to immediate diseconomies of scale.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scale Direction Reversal): Rapidly rising LRATC favors many small firms, not a single large firm; natural monopoly requires falling LRATC.

options_template.text: Long-Run Average Total Cost declines continuously across the entire relevant range of market demand.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Continuous economies of scale (falling LRATC over all relevant market quantities) allow one large firm to serve the entire market at lower average cost than multiple competing firms.

options_template.text: Marginal cost exceeds Long-Run Average Total Cost at every positive level of output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MC-ATC Relationship Error): Whenever LRATC is declining, marginal cost must lie strictly below average total cost (MC < LRATC), not above it.

options_template.text: Fixed costs are zero while variable costs increase exponentially with every additional customer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Misconception): Natural monopolies are driven by massive fixed infrastructure costs spread across large output, not zero fixed costs with exploding variable costs.

questions.title: How Network Effects Create Barriers to Entry
questions.prompt_template: Why do network effects function as a barrier to entry in digital platforms and communications services?

hints.text: Think about how one user's benefit from joining a platform depends on how many other people already use it.
Consider why a new entrant with a tiny user base struggles to attract customers away from a large incumbent network.

options_template.text: Because government agencies automatically issue 20-year patents to every online platform.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal vs. Network Barrier Confusion): Patents are government-created legal barriers, whereas network effects arise from demand-side user interdependence.

options_template.text: Because network platforms own exclusive physical rights to every mineral required for computer hardware.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Resource-Control Confusion): Owning a physical input is exclusive resource control, not a network effect.

options_template.text: Because adding more users causes the platform's value per user to fall, deterring new customers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Congestion vs. Network Effect Reversal): Falling value per user is congestion; network effects occur when value per user rises as more people join.

options_template.text: Because each user derives greater value as the platform's user base grows, making it difficult for smaller entrants to draw users away.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Positive network effects increase user value with network size, locking in customers and creating a steep hurdle for smaller rivals trying to achieve critical mass.

questions.title: Output Effect and Price Effect Under Single Pricing
questions.prompt_template: For a single-price monopolist facing a downward-sloping market demand curve, why is Marginal Revenue strictly less than Price (MR < P) for every unit beyond the first?

hints.text: Decompose the change in Total Revenue when selling one more unit into the gain on the new unit and the loss on existing units.
Under single pricing, lowering the price to attract an additional buyer also lowers the price collected on all earlier units.

options_template.text: Because the monopolist must pay higher per-unit wages each time it expands production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost vs. Revenue Confusion): Rising input prices affect marginal cost (MC), not the relationship between marginal revenue (MR) and price (P).

options_template.text: Because selling an extra unit requires lowering the price on all prior units as well, creating a negative price effect that offsets part of the positive output effect.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Marginal revenue equals the positive output effect (+P) plus the negative price effect (-Q * |Delta P|), so MR lies strictly below P for all Q > 0.

options_template.text: Because a single-price monopolist faces a horizontal demand curve where price never changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Taker Transfer): A horizontal firm demand curve applies to perfect competition, where the price effect is zero and MR = P.

options_template.text: Because total revenue always decreases whenever a monopolist sells an additional unit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR < P vs. MR < 0 Conflation): MR < P holds everywhere for Q > 0, yet MR is still positive (so total revenue rises) along the elastic upper half of demand.

questions.title: Why a Monopolist Avoids the Inelastic Region of Demand
questions.prompt_template: Why will a profit-maximizing single-price monopolist with non-negative marginal cost (MC >= 0) NEVER operate on the inelastic portion of its market demand curve?

hints.text: Check the sign of Marginal Revenue (MR) when demand is price inelastic (|e_d| < 1).
Think about what happens to both Total Revenue and Total Cost if the firm cuts output by one unit while MR < 0.

options_template.text: Because price is legally capped in the inelastic region by antitrust statutes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Fabrication): Avoiding the inelastic region is a purely mathematical result of profit maximization, not a legal restriction.

options_template.text: Because marginal revenue exceeds price in the inelastic region, causing costs to spiral.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR Ordering Error): For a single-price monopolist, MR never exceeds P; in the inelastic region, MR is actually negative.

options_template.text: Because MR < 0 in the inelastic region, so reducing output raises total revenue while lowering total cost, strictly increasing profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Along the inelastic portion of demand (|e_d| < 1), MR is negative; cutting output simultaneously increases TR and reduces TC (since MC >= 0), moving the firm into the elastic region where MR = MC >= 0.

options_template.text: Because consumers refuse to purchase any units at all once demand becomes inelastic.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Demand Misconception): Quantities are actually relatively large (and prices low) in the inelastic lower half of linear demand; the issue is negative marginal revenue, not zero sales.

questions.title: The Two-Step Monopoly Profit-Maximization Rule
questions.prompt_template: How does a single-price monopolist determine its profit-maximizing output (Q_M) and price (P_M)?

hints.text: Remember that choosing output and reading the market-clearing price are two distinct steps.
First equate marginal revenue to marginal cost to find Q_M, then use the curve that reflects buyers' maximum willingness to pay.

options_template.text: Choose Q_M where MR = MC, then move vertically up from Q_M to the market demand curve to set P_M.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Equating MR = MC identifies the profit-maximizing quantity Q_M, and the demand curve gives the highest price P_M consumers will pay for that quantity.

options_template.text: Choose Q_M where MR = MC, and charge a price equal to the vertical value at the MR = MC intersection.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR = MC Price-Reading Fallacy): The MR = MC intersection determines only quantity Q_M; charging P = MR = MC leaves substantial willing-to-pay revenue on the table because D lies above MR.

options_template.text: Choose Q_M where P = MC, then read P_M vertically down to the Marginal Revenue curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Rule Misapplication): Setting P = MC identifies the socially efficient competitive output Q_C, not the monopolist's profit-maximizing output Q_M.

options_template.text: Choose Q_M where MR = 0 to maximize total revenue, then set P_M equal to Average Total Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Maximization Fallacy): Maximizing total revenue (MR = 0) ignores production costs whenever MC > 0, and setting P = ATC forces zero profit rather than maximum profit.

questions.title: Can a Pure Monopolist Earn Economic Losses?
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately describes the profitability of a pure monopolist in the short run?

hints.text: Does having no competitors force consumers to pay more than the firm's average total cost?
Compare the profit-maximizing price P_M against Average Total Cost (ATC) and Average Variable Cost (AVC).

options_template.text: A pure monopolist is guaranteed positive economic profit because it can charge any price it chooses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Guaranteed-Profit Myth): Even a sole seller is constrained by market demand; if demand lies below ATC at all quantities, the monopolist cannot earn positive profit.

options_template.text: A pure monopolist must earn zero economic profit in the long run because rivals automatically enter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Long-Run Transfer): Barriers to entry block rival entry, allowing a profitable monopolist to sustain positive economic profit in the long run.

options_template.text: A pure monopolist always shuts down immediately in the short run whenever P_M < ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shutdown Threshold Error): Just like any firm, a monopolist shuts down in the short run only if P_M < AVC; if AVC <= P_M < ATC, operating covers variable costs and part of fixed costs.

options_template.text: A pure monopolist suffers an economic loss if P_M < ATC at Q_M, and shuts down in the short run if P_M < AVC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Market power lets a monopolist pick the best point on the demand curve, not ignore weak demand or high costs; it loses money when P_M < ATC and shuts down in the short run when P_M < AVC.

questions.title: Economic Meaning of Monopoly Deadweight Loss
questions.prompt_template: Why does a single-price monopoly generate Deadweight Loss (DWL) relative to perfect competition?

hints.text: Compare the monopolist's price P_M and output Q_M against the competitive benchmark where P = MC.
Focus on the units between Q_M and Q_C that are not produced even though buyers value them above their marginal cost.

options_template.text: Because every dollar of economic profit earned by the monopolist is destroyed rather than transferred.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer vs. Loss Confusion): Monopoly profit is a transfer from consumer surplus to producer surplus, not deadweight loss; DWL comes strictly from unproduced trades.

options_template.text: Because restricting output to Q_M < Q_C prevents mutually beneficial trades where consumers' marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost (P > MC).
options_template.feedback: Correct. By holding output below Q_C so that P_M > MC, the monopolist leaves unproduced units whose value to buyers exceeds the cost of producing them, destroying social surplus.

options_template.text: Because monopolists always produce more output than perfectly competitive firms (Q_M > Q_C), wasting resources.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overproduction Reversal): Single-price monopolists underproduce relative to perfect competition (Q_M < Q_C), not overproduce.

options_template.text: Because consumers pay a lower price under monopoly than under perfect competition, causing excess demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Direction Reversal): Monopolists charge a higher price (P_M > P_C), not a lower price, than a perfectly competitive market with the same cost structure.

questions.title: Three Necessary Conditions for Price Discrimination
questions.prompt_template: Which three conditions must ALL hold for a firm to practice price discrimination successfully?

hints.text: Ask what the firm needs regarding pricing power, customer differences, and secondary-market resale.
Even if a firm has market power and identifies different groups, low-price buyers must not be able to resell to high-price buyers.

options_template.text: Perfectly horizontal firm demand, identical buyer elasticities, and unrestricted resale across consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complete Condition Inversion): Each element listed here prevents price discrimination—price takers have no market power, identical elasticities offer no segmentation basis, and resale destroys price gaps.

options_template.text: Rising marginal cost, government price ceilings, and zero fixed costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrelevant Cost/Policy Conditions): Price discrimination can occur with constant MC and positive fixed costs, and does not require government price ceilings.

options_template.text: Market power, the ability to segment buyers by willingness to pay (elasticity), and the ability to prevent arbitrage (resale).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A firm must face downward-sloping demand (market power), separate customers with different elasticities, and block low-price buyers from reselling to high-price buyers.

options_template.text: Different production costs for each buyer, free entry of competitors, and uniform marginal revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Difference Misconception): Price differences justified by cost differences are NOT price discrimination, and free entry eliminates the required market power.

questions.title: Distinguishing First-, Second-, and Third-Degree Price Discrimination
questions.prompt_template: A wholesale warehouse club offers lower per-unit prices to shoppers who buy 24-packs rather than single items, while a movie theater offers discounted tickets to customers showing a valid student ID. How are these two pricing strategies classified?

hints.text: Check whether customers self-select from a menu of quantities or are separated by an observable demographic characteristic.
Quantity discounts rely on self-selection (second-degree), whereas observable group identifiers like student IDs represent third-degree price discrimination.

options_template.text: The bulk pack discount is second-degree price discrimination; the student ID discount is third-degree price discrimination.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Second-degree price discrimination uses quantity tiers or product menus so buyers self-select, whereas third-degree price discrimination segments buyers using observable group traits such as student status.

options_template.text: The bulk pack discount is first-degree price discrimination; the student ID discount is second-degree price discrimination.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Degree Shift Error): First-degree (perfect) price discrimination charges every single customer their exact individual willingness to pay, not a menu of bulk prices.

options_template.text: Both pricing practices are examples of first-degree (perfect) price discrimination.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect Discrimination Overgeneralization): Neither bulk packs nor group discounts extract every buyer's exact individual reservation price.

options_template.text: The bulk pack discount is third-degree price discrimination; the student ID discount is second-degree price discrimination.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Second/Third-Degree Reversal): Second-degree relies on quantity or menu self-selection (bulk packs), while third-degree relies on observable buyer categories (student IDs).

questions.title: Welfare Outcomes Under First-Degree (Perfect) Price Discrimination
questions.prompt_template: Compared to a single-price monopoly with the same demand and constant marginal cost, how does first-degree (perfect) price discrimination affect output, Consumer Surplus, and Deadweight Loss?

hints.text: When a firm charges each buyer their exact willingness to pay, does it have to cut prices on earlier units to sell an extra unit?
Without a negative price effect, MR = P, so the firm expands output all the way to P = MC while capturing every dollar of buyer surplus.

options_template.text: Output falls further below Q_M, Consumer Surplus rises, and Deadweight Loss doubles.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output & Welfare Reversal): Eliminating the price effect encourages the firm to expand output to Q_C, which eliminates deadweight loss rather than doubling it.

options_template.text: Output expands to the competitive level Q_C, Consumer Surplus is maximized, and Deadweight Loss falls to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect Competition Conflation): Although output reaches Q_C and DWL = $0, buyers pay their exact maximum willingness to pay, leaving Consumer Surplus at $0 rather than maximized.

options_template.text: Output remains stuck at Q_M, Consumer Surplus falls to zero, and Deadweight Loss remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Output Assumption): Because the firm no longer discounts earlier units to make marginal sales, it profitably sells every unit up to Q_C where WTP = MC.

options_template.text: Output expands to the competitive level Q_C, Deadweight Loss falls to zero, and Consumer Surplus falls to zero as the monopolist captures 100% of total surplus.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under perfect price discrimination, MR = P, so output reaches Q_C with zero deadweight loss, while the firm converts the entire social surplus into economic profit (CS = $0).

questions.title: Interpreting the Lerner Index of Market Power
questions.prompt_template: How is the Lerner Index (L) defined, and what value does it take in a perfectly competitive market?

hints.text: Express the firm's markup above marginal cost as a fraction of its price, and recall how price relates to marginal cost under perfect competition.
In perfect competition, P = MC and the firm's perceived price elasticity of demand approaches infinity.

options_template.text: L = (P - MC) / MC, which equals 1 in a perfectly competitive market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Denominator & Benchmark Error): The Lerner Index divides the markup by price P—not MC—and equals 0 (not 1) when P = MC.

options_template.text: L = (P - MC) / P = 1 / |e_d|, which equals 0 in a perfectly competitive market.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Lerner Index measures percentage price-cost margin (P - MC) / P, equals 1 / |e_d| at a monopolist's optimum, and equals 0 in perfect competition where P = MC and |e_d| approaches infinity.

options_template.text: L = (P - ATC) / P = |e_d|, which equals infinity in a perfectly competitive market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (ATC & Inverted Elasticity Error): The Lerner Index uses marginal cost MC rather than ATC and equals the reciprocal of elasticity (1 / |e_d|), not |e_d|.

options_template.text: L = MC / P, which equals 0 whenever a monopolist maximizes profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Markup Complement Confusion): MC / P is 1 - L; when a firm has market power and P > MC > 0, L lies strictly between 0 and 1.

questions.title: Intercepts and Slopes of Linear Demand and Marginal Revenue
questions.prompt_template: On a standard price-quantity graph, a single-price monopolist faces a linear inverse demand curve with a vertical choke price of $100 and a horizontal choke quantity of 50 units. Where does the corresponding Marginal Revenue (MR) curve start and where does it cross the horizontal quantity axis?

hints.text: Recall how the vertical intercept and slope of MR = a - 2bQ compare to linear inverse demand P = a - bQ.
Doubling the downward slope from the same vertical starting point cuts the horizontal intercept in half.

options_template.text: It starts at $50 on the vertical axis and crosses the horizontal axis at Q = 50.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Halved Vertical Intercept Error): MR shares the exact same vertical choke intercept ($100) as demand; halving the vertical intercept violates MR(0) = P(0).

options_template.text: It starts at $100 on the vertical axis and crosses the horizontal axis at Q = 50.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identical Curve Error): Crossing at Q = 50 would make MR identical to the demand curve, ignoring the negative price effect under single pricing.

options_template.text: It starts at $100 on the vertical axis and crosses the horizontal axis at Q = 25.
options_template.feedback: Correct. For linear demand P = 100 - 2Q, MR = 100 - 4Q shares the vertical intercept ($100), falls twice as steeply, and reaches zero at the exact midpoint quantity Q = 25.

options_template.text: It starts at $200 on the vertical axis and crosses the horizontal axis at Q = 25.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Doubled Intercept Error): Only the slope coefficient b is doubled in MR = a - 2bQ; the choke price intercept a remains $100.

questions.title: Mapping Elasticity Regions to Marginal Revenue on a Graph
questions.prompt_template: In a graph of linear inverse demand P = 100 - 2Q and MR = 100 - 4Q, the MR curve crosses the horizontal axis at Q = 25 (where P = $50). How does price elasticity of demand behave to the left and right of Q = 25?

hints.text: Connect the sign of Marginal Revenue (MR > 0, MR = 0, MR < 0) to the elasticity of demand along a straight-line demand curve.
Remember that total revenue rises when MR > 0 (price cuts expand revenue along the elastic segment) and falls when MR < 0.

options_template.text: Demand is elastic (|e_d| > 1) for 0 < Q < 25 where MR > 0, unit elastic (|e_d| = 1) at Q = 25 where MR = 0, and inelastic (|e_d| < 1) for Q > 25 where MR < 0.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Above the midpoint (Q < 25), lowering price raises TR (MR > 0, elastic); at Q = 25, TR peaks (MR = 0, unit elastic); below the midpoint (Q > 25), lowering price reduces TR (MR < 0, inelastic).

options_template.text: Demand is inelastic (|e_d| < 1) for 0 < Q < 25 where MR > 0, and elastic (|e_d| > 1) for Q > 25 where MR < 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elastic/Inelastic Region Reversal): At high prices and low quantities on a linear demand curve, percentage quantity changes are large relative to percentage price changes, making the upper half elastic—not inelastic.

options_template.text: Price elasticity of demand is constant at |e_d| = 2 everywhere along the linear demand curve because the slope is constant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Elasticity Conflation): A constant slope (-2) does NOT mean constant elasticity; elasticity varies from infinity at the vertical intercept to 0 at the horizontal intercept.

options_template.text: Demand is elastic everywhere from Q = 0 to Q = 50 because the demand curve slopes downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-Slope Misconception): Every downward-sloping linear demand curve passes through elastic, unit-elastic, and inelastic ranges as quantity increases.

questions.title: Locating Equilibrium Price and Quantity on a Monopoly Diagram
questions.prompt_template: On a monopoly diagram with linear demand P = 100 - 2Q, MR = 100 - 4Q, and constant MC = $20, the MR and MC curves intersect at the point (Q = 20, $20), while the demand curve passes through (Q = 20, $60) and crosses MC at (Q = 40, $20). Which coordinate pair represents the unregulated single-price monopoly equilibrium (Q_M, P_M)?

hints.text: Apply the two-step rule graphically: find Q_M at the MR = MC crossing, then move straight up to the demand curve.
Do not confuse the open-circle MR = MC crossing with the equilibrium price point E_M on the demand curve.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR = MC Price-Reading Fallacy): The coordinate (20, $20) is where MR = MC, which determines quantity Q_M = 20, not the price buyers pay on the demand curve.
Correct. Equating MR = MC sets Q_M = 20, and reading vertically up to the demand curve at Q = 20 gives the profit-maximizing price P_M = $60.
Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Benchmark Confusion): The intersection of Demand and MC at (40, $20) is the perfectly competitive equilibrium (Q_C, P_C), not the monopoly equilibrium.
Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Maximization Confusion): The midpoint (25, $50) maximizes total revenue where MR = 0, ignoring the positive marginal cost of $20 per unit.

questions.title: Identifying Consumer Surplus, Profit, and Deadweight Loss Regions
questions.prompt_template: In a standard single-price monopoly graph with constant MC = ATC, which geometric area corresponds specifically to the Harberger Deadweight Loss (DWL) triangle?

hints.text: Locate the unproduced units between Q_M and Q_C on the horizontal axis.
For each unproduced unit between Q_M and Q_C, the lost surplus equals the vertical gap between the demand curve and the MC curve.

options_template.text: The triangle bounded above by the demand curve, below by the horizontal line at P_M, and on the left by the vertical axis from Q = 0 to Q_M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumer Surplus Confusion): That upper triangle above P_M from Q = 0 to Q_M represents Consumer Surplus under monopoly (CS_M), not Deadweight Loss.

options_template.text: The rectangle between P_M and MC = ATC extending horizontally from Q = 0 to Q_M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profit Transfer Confusion): That rectangle measures monopoly economic profit—a transfer from consumers to the firm—rather than lost social surplus.

options_template.text: The triangle bounded above by the MR curve and below by the MC curve from Q = 0 to Q_M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR-Area Misidentification): Welfare analysis compares buyers' willingness to pay (Demand) against social cost (MC), not MR against MC.

options_template.text: The triangle bounded above by the demand curve, below by the MC curve, and extending horizontally between Q_M and Q_C.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Between Q_M and Q_C, Demand lies above MC, so the triangle enclosed by Demand, MC, and the vertical line at Q_M captures the total lost social surplus (DWL).

questions.title: Graphical Ratio of Monopoly to Competitive Output Under Constant MC
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a market has a linear downward-sloping demand curve and a horizontal (constant) marginal cost curve strictly below the choke price. Visually, how does the monopoly quantity Q_M always compare to the competitive quantity Q_C?

hints.text: Compare the slope of MR = a - 2bQ with the slope of Demand P = a - bQ starting from the same vertical gap (a - c) above MC.
Because MR falls twice as fast as Demand from the vertical intercept down to the constant MC line, it hits MC halfway to Q_C.

options_template.text: Q_M is always one-third of Q_C.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Factor Error): Because MR has twice—not three times—the slope of linear demand, it reaches the horizontal MC line at half of Q_C, not one-third.

options_template.text: Q_M is always three-quarters of Q_C.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus Fraction Confusion): Three-quarters is the fraction of total competitive surplus preserved as CS_M + Profit (3/4 of CS_C), not the ratio of outputs.

options_template.text: Q_M is always exactly one-half of Q_C.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since MR = a - 2bQ falls twice as steeply as P = a - bQ from the same intercept a, Q_M = (a - c)/(2b) is always exactly half of Q_C = (a - c)/b.

options_template.text: Q_M equals Q_C whenever marginal cost is constant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-MC Efficiency Fallacy): Constant MC eliminates rising-cost curvature, but single pricing still forces MR < P, so the monopolist still restricts output to half of Q_C.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of an Upward Shift in Constant Marginal Cost
questions.prompt_template: A single-price monopolist operates with linear demand and constant marginal cost. If an increase in per-unit input prices shifts the horizontal MC curve upward (while remaining below the choke price), how do the monopoly graph's equilibrium quantity Q_M, price P_M, and Consumer Surplus change?

hints.text: Trace the new intersection of the higher horizontal MC curve with the unchanged downward-sloping MR curve.
Moving up along the downward-sloping MR curve moves Q_M to the left, which moves the equilibrium point up and left along the demand curve.

options_template.text: Q_M decreases, P_M increases, and Consumer Surplus decreases.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher MC line intersects the downward-sloping MR curve at a smaller quantity Q_M; reading up to the unchanged demand curve yields a higher price P_M and a smaller Consumer Surplus triangle.

options_template.text: Q_M increases, P_M decreases, and Consumer Surplus increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Direction Reversal): An upward MC shift raises per-unit costs, reducing—not expanding—the number of units where MR exceeds MC.

options_template.text: Q_M decreases, P_M remains unchanged, and Consumer Surplus remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Rigidity Assumption): Because the monopolist moves up a downward-sloping demand curve as Q_M falls, the market-clearing price P_M must rise.

options_template.text: Q_M remains unchanged because a monopolist passes 100% of cost increases to buyers without reducing sales.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic Pass-Through Myth): Even a monopolist faces downward-sloping demand; raising price to pass along higher MC necessarily reduces quantity demanded.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Parallel Rightward Shift in Market Demand
questions.prompt_template: If rising consumer income causes a single-price monopolist's linear market demand curve to shift outward in parallel (higher vertical choke price, same slope) while constant MC stays unchanged, what happens on the graph?

hints.text: Remember that whenever the demand curve shifts right, the associated MR curve shifts with it.
Compare the old and new intersections of MR with the horizontal MC line, and then read the new price off the higher demand curve.

options_template.text: The demand curve shifts right, MR stays fixed, so Q_M stays unchanged while P_M rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frozen-MR Error): Because MR is derived directly from demand (MR = a - 2bQ), raising the demand intercept a shifts the MR curve upward/rightward by the same vertical distance.

options_template.text: Both D and MR shift outward, causing both Q_M and P_M to increase.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher vertical demand intercept raises both D and MR, moving the MR = MC crossing rightward (higher Q_M) and raising the profit-maximizing price P_M along the higher demand curve.

options_template.text: Both D and MR shift outward, causing Q_M to increase and P_M to fall to MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Price Convergence Error): Stronger demand does not turn a monopolist into a price taker; P_M = (a + c)/2 rises by half the vertical demand shift.

options_template.text: Both D and MR shift outward, causing Q_M to fall as the monopolist restricts sales to capture higher prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output-Restriction Misconception): When MR shifts right against a flat MC curve, marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost at the old Q_M, making it profitable to expand output.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Lump-Sum Fixed Cost Increase
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a city imposes an annual lump-sum license fee (a pure fixed cost) on a profitable local monopolist, leaving its economic profit still positive. How does this fee alter the curves and equilibrium on the monopoly diagram?

hints.text: Determine which cost curve shifts when fixed costs rise: MC, ATC, or both?
Since the profit-maximizing quantity depends only on MR and MC, check whether either of those curves moves.

options_template.text: Both MC and ATC shift upward, reducing Q_M and raising P_M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed vs. Marginal Cost Conflation): A lump-sum fixed fee does not depend on output Q, so it leaves MC completely unchanged and shifts only ATC upward.

options_template.text: The MR curve shifts downward, causing the monopolist to raise P_M to pass the fee to consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Cost Cross-Contamination): A lump-sum cost change affects the firm's cost structure (ATC), not consumer demand or marginal revenue.

options_template.text: ATC shifts upward and the monopolist expands Q_M to spread the higher fixed cost across more units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Spreading Fallacy): Expanding output beyond MR = MC adds less revenue than marginal cost, which would reduce profit even further regardless of fixed costs.

options_template.text: ATC shifts upward while MC and MR stay unchanged, so Q_M and P_M remain unchanged and the profit rectangle shrinks vertically.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A lump-sum fixed cost shifts only ATC upward; because MR and MC are unaffected (and profit stays positive), Q_M and P_M do not change, while the vertical height of the profit box (P_M - ATC) narrows.

questions.title: Comparing Unregulated, Fair-Return, and Marginal-Cost Pricing Points
questions.prompt_template: On a natural monopoly diagram where LRATC slopes downward across all relevant market quantities and constant MC lies strictly below LRATC, how are the three key policy points ordered from LEFT to RIGHT along the horizontal quantity axis?

hints.text: Identify the three intersection rules: MR = MC (unregulated), Demand = LRATC (fair-return), and Demand = MC (marginal-cost pricing).
Follow the downward-sloping demand curve from highest price to lowest price as quantity expands.

options_template.text: Unregulated monopoly (MR = MC) furthest left, fair-return pricing (P = LRATC) in the middle, and marginal-cost pricing (P = MC) furthest right.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because MR lies below Demand and MC lies below declining LRATC, moving down the demand curve passes unregulated Q_M first, then fair-return Q_FR (where P = LRATC), and finally allocatively efficient Q_MC (where P = MC).

options_template.text: Marginal-cost pricing (P = MC) furthest left, fair-return pricing (P = LRATC) in the middle, and unregulated monopoly (MR = MC) furthest right.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity Ordering Reversal): Lowering price from the unregulated monopoly level toward MC moves down the demand curve to larger—not smaller—quantities.

options_template.text: Unregulated monopoly (MR = MC) furthest left, marginal-cost pricing (P = MC) in the middle, and fair-return pricing (P = LRATC) furthest right.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MC-LRATC Position Reversal): Because LRATC is falling, MC must lie below LRATC, so Demand crosses LRATC at a higher price and smaller quantity than where Demand crosses MC.

options_template.text: Fair-return pricing (P = LRATC) and marginal-cost pricing (P = MC) coincide at the exact same quantity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Minimum-ATC Assumption): MC equals LRATC only at the minimum point of LRATC; in a natural monopoly, LRATC is still declining across market demand, so MC < LRATC throughout.

questions.title: Graphical Second-Order Condition When MC Intersects MR Twice
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a monopolist has a U-shaped marginal cost curve that intersects its downward-sloping Marginal Revenue curve at two positive quantities: Q_1 (where MC crosses MR from above) and Q_2 (where MC crosses MR from below). Which quantity maximizes profit, and why?

hints.text: Check whether MR > MC or MR < MC just to the right of each intersection.
Profit rises whenever expanding output adds more to revenue than to cost (MR > MC), and peaks only where MC rises above MR.

options_template.text: Q_1 maximizes profit because the firm should stop at the very first quantity where MR = MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (First-Crossing Heuristic): At Q_1, MC crosses MR from above, meaning MR > MC immediately past Q_1; Q_1 is a local profit minimum rather than a maximum.

options_template.text: Both Q_1 and Q_2 yield the exact same maximum profit because MR = MC holds at both points.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (FOC-Only Sufficiency Fallacy): Equating MR = MC is only the First-Order Condition; the Second-Order Condition (MR' < MC') is required to distinguish a maximum from a minimum.

options_template.text: Q_2 maximizes profit because MC intersects MR from below, ensuring MR > MC before Q_2 and MR < MC after Q_2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Second-Order Condition (pi''(Q) = MR' - MC' < 0) requires MC to cut MR from below so that units up to Q_2 add profit and units beyond Q_2 reduce profit.

options_template.text: Neither quantity can maximize profit because a monopolist can only maximize profit when MC is horizontal.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-MC Restriction): Constant MC is a simplifying assumption in introductory diagrams, not a requirement for profit maximization.

questions.title: How Perfect Price Discrimination Transforms the Monopoly Diagram
questions.prompt_template: On a monopoly diagram with linear demand and constant MC = ATC, how do the curves and shaded welfare areas change when the firm switches from single pricing to first-degree (perfect) price discrimination?

hints.text: Ask what happens to the Marginal Revenue curve when selling an extra unit no longer requires cutting the price on prior units.
Once MR coincides with Demand, trace the new intersection with MC and see who captures the entire triangle between Demand and MC.

options_template.text: The MR curve shifts below its single-price position, output falls, and the Deadweight Loss triangle expands.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR Shift Direction Error): Removing the negative price effect shifts MR upward to match the Demand curve, expanding output and eliminating DWL.

options_template.text: The MR curve coincides with the Demand curve, output expands from Q_M to Q_C, the DWL triangle disappears, and the entire triangle between Demand and MC becomes monopoly profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under perfect price discrimination, each unit sells at its buyer's willingness to pay (MR = P), so output reaches Q_C, DWL shrinks to $0, CS shrinks to $0, and profit equals the full surplus triangle.

options_template.text: The MC curve shifts downward to zero while the Demand curve stays unchanged, transferring profit back to consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Curve Distortion): Price discrimination alters pricing and marginal revenue, not the firm's marginal production cost.

options_template.text: The MR curve coincides with the Demand curve, output expands to Q_C, and Consumer Surplus expands to fill the entire triangle between Demand and MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Recipient Reversal): Because every consumer pays their exact reservation price, the firm—not consumers—captures the entire triangle between Demand and MC.

questions.title: Reading Two-Panel Third-Degree Price Discrimination Graphs
questions.prompt_template: In a two-panel graph for a campus theater with constant MC = $4 per ticket, Panel (a) shows the less elastic General Public demand curve (D_1, MR_1) and Panel (b) shows the more elastic Student demand curve (D_2, MR_2). How does the theater find its profit-maximizing prices graphically?

hints.text: Look at how the common horizontal MC = $4 line intersects MR_1 in Panel (a) and MR_2 in Panel (b).
In each separated segment, apply the standard monopoly two-step rule independently: MR_i = MC for quantity, then up to D_i for price.

options_template.text: Equate MR_1 = $4 in Panel (a) and MR_2 = $4 in Panel (b) independently, then read vertically up to D_1 and D_2, yielding a higher price for the less elastic general public and a lower price for students.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With constant MC and no resale, setting MR_1 = MC and MR_2 = MC independently maximizes combined profit and places a larger markup on the less elastic segment.

options_template.text: Equate D_1 = $4 in Panel (a) and D_2 = $4 in Panel (b), charging $4 in both panels.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Pricing Application): Setting P = MC in both segments yields zero economic profit and fails to exploit market power.

options_template.text: Equate MR_1 = $4 in Panel (a) and MR_2 = $4 in Panel (b), yielding a lower price for the less elastic general public and a higher price for more elastic students.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Elasticity Pricing): The inverse-elasticity rule dictates a higher—not lower—price for the less elastic (more price-insensitive) group.

options_template.text: Equate MR_1 = 0 in Panel (a) and MR_2 = 0 in Panel (b) so both segments reach unit elasticity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-MC Revenue Maximization): Equating MR_i = 0 ignores the positive marginal cost ($4 per ticket); with MC > 0, both optimal points lie in the elastic region (|e_i| > 1).

questions.title: Graphing a Short-Run Loss-Minimizing Monopolist
questions.prompt_template: On a short-run monopoly diagram, suppose that at the quantity Q_M where MR = MC, the Demand curve lies below the ATC curve but above the AVC curve (AVC < P_M < ATC). What does the rectangle between ATC and P_M from Q = 0 to Q_M represent, and what should the monopolist do in the short run?

hints.text: Compare P_M to ATC to determine profit vs. loss, and compare P_M to AVC to evaluate the short-run shutdown rule.
Whenever price exceeds AVC, operating generates revenue above variable costs that helps pay down unavoidable fixed costs.

options_template.text: It represents positive economic profit, so the monopolist should expand output beyond Q_M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (ATC-Price Ordering Reversal): When ATC lies above P_M, average cost exceeds price per unit, meaning the firm suffers an economic loss rather than earning positive profit.

options_template.text: It represents an economic loss, so the monopolist must shut down immediately in the short run to reduce losses to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Recovery Illusion): Shutting down does not eliminate fixed costs in the short run; because P_M > AVC, producing Q_M loses less than shutting down.

options_template.text: It represents the firm's minimum short-run economic loss, and the monopolist should continue producing Q_M in the short run because P_M > AVC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since P_M < ATC, the rectangle (ATC - P_M) * Q_M is an economic loss; because P_M > AVC, staying open covers all variable costs plus part of fixed costs, minimizing short-run loss.

options_template.text: It represents Deadweight Loss, and the monopolist breaks even because MR = MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR = MC Break-Even Myth): Equating MR = MC maximizes profit or minimizes loss; it does NOT guarantee zero loss when ATC lies above the demand curve.

questions.title: Deriving Marginal Revenue and Revenue-Maximizing Quantity
questions.prompt_template: A single-price monopolist faces the linear inverse market demand curve P = 160 - 4Q. What are its Marginal Revenue equation MR(Q) and the quantity Q that maximizes Total Revenue?

hints.text: For linear inverse demand P = a - bQ, keep the vertical intercept a unchanged and double the slope coefficient b.
Total Revenue reaches its maximum where MR(Q) = 0.

options_template.text: MR = 160 - 4Q; Q = 40 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Forgotten Slope Doubling): Setting MR = P ignores the negative price effect; MR must have twice the slope (-8Q), not the same slope (-4Q).

options_template.text: MR = 160 - 8Q; Q = 20 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. Keeping the vertical intercept (160) and doubling the slope coefficient (2 * 4 = 8) yields MR = 160 - 8Q; setting 160 - 8Q = 0 gives the TR-maximizing midpoint Q = 20 units.

options_template.text: MR = 80 - 4Q; Q = 20 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Halved Intercept Error): Although 80 - 4Q = 0 happens to give Q = 20, MR must share the demand choke intercept ($160), not halve it to $80.

options_template.text: MR = 320 - 8Q; Q = 40 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Doubled Both Intercept and Slope): Only the slope coefficient is doubled when moving from P = a - bQ to MR = a - 2bQ; multiplying the intercept by 2 doubles the choke price erroneously.

questions.topic: Output Effect and Price Effect Calculation
questions.title: Decomposing Discrete Marginal Revenue into Output and Price Effects
questions.prompt_template: A patented software tool faces linear inverse demand P = 90 - 2Q. When the monopolist expands sales from Q = 10 units to Q = 11 units under single pricing, what are the output effect, the price effect, and the net discrete Marginal Revenue?

hints.text: First calculate the price at Q = 10 and at Q = 11, then compute Total Revenue at both quantities to check your decomposition.
The output effect is the price of the 11th unit (+P_11), and the price effect is the price discount applied to the 10 prior units (-10 * |Delta P|).

options_template.text: Output effect = +$68, price effect = -$20, net MR = +$48
options_template.feedback: Correct. At Q = 10, P = $70 (TR = $700); at Q = 11, P = $68 (TR = $748). Selling the 11th unit adds +$68 (output effect), while discounting the 10 prior units by $2 subtracts -$20 (price effect), leaving net MR = $68 - $20 = +$48.

options_template.text: Output effect = +$68, price effect = -$22, net MR = +$46
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Applied Discount to New Unit): The $2 discount applies only to the 10 prior units (-10 * $2 = -$20), not all 11 units, because the 11th unit is already counted at the lower price ($68).

options_template.text: Output effect = +$70, price effect = -$20, net MR = +$50
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Used Prior Price as Output Effect): The 11th unit sells at the new lower price ($68), not the old price ($70); using $70 overstates discrete MR by $2.

options_template.text: Output effect = +$68, price effect = $0, net MR = +$68
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Taker Omission): Under single pricing, the price effect is zero only for a competitive price taker; here, discounting 10 prior units reduces revenue by -$20.

questions.title: Solving for Monopoly Output and Price Under Constant MC
questions.prompt_template: A single-price monopolist faces linear inverse market demand P = 140 - 2Q (so MR = 140 - 4Q) and operates with constant Marginal Cost MC = $20. What are the monopolist's profit-maximizing quantity (Q_M) and price (P_M)?

hints.text: Step 1: Set MR = MC to solve for Q_M.
Step 2: Substitute Q_M into the inverse demand equation P = 140 - 2Q—not into MR—to find P_M.

options_template.text: Q_M = 30 units, P_M = $20
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR = MC Price-Reading Fallacy): Q_M = 30 is correct, but $20 is the value of MR and MC at Q = 30; you must plug Q_M = 30 into demand P = 140 - 2(30) = $80.

options_template.text: Q_M = 60 units, P_M = $20
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive P = MC Substitution): Setting 140 - 2Q = 20 solves for the perfectly competitive benchmark (Q_C = 60, P_C = $20) rather than the monopoly optimum.

options_template.text: Q_M = 30 units, P_M = $80
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting MR = MC gives 140 - 4Q_M = 20 -> 4Q_M = 120 -> Q_M = 30 units; substituting into inverse demand gives P_M = 140 - 2(30) = $80.

options_template.text: Q_M = 35 units, P_M = $70
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Maximization Fallacy): Setting MR = 0 (140 - 4Q = 0) yields Q = 35 and P = $70, which maximizes total revenue but ignores the $20 marginal cost.

questions.title: Calculating Monopoly Economic Profit With Positive Fixed Cost
questions.prompt_template: A monopolist faces inverse demand P = 110 - 5Q (so MR = 110 - 10Q), constant Marginal Cost MC = $10 per unit, and Fixed Cost FC = $300. What is the monopolist's maximum economic profit?

hints.text: Find Q_M from MR = MC and P_M from inverse demand, then compute Total Revenue (P_M * Q_M) and Total Cost (FC + MC * Q_M).
Remember that economic profit equals TR - TC = (P_M - ATC) * Q_M, which must subtract Fixed Cost as well as Variable Cost.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Fixed Cost): Computing (P_M - MC) * Q_M = ($60 - $10) * 10 = $500 ignores the $300 fixed cost; subtracting FC leaves $200.
Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Profit Conflation): $600 is Total Revenue ($60 * 10) before deducting Total Cost ($300 + $10 * 10 = $400).
Diagnostic fallacy (Triangle Formula on Profit Box): Profit is a rectangle (P_M - ATC) * Q_M = ($60 - $40) * 10 = $200, not a triangle; multiplying by 1/2 erroneously halves profit to $100.
Correct. Setting 110 - 10Q_M = 10 gives Q_M = 10 and P_M = 110 - 5(10) = $60. Total Revenue is $60 * 10 = $600 and Total Cost is $300 + $10(10) = $400, yielding economic profit of $600 - $400 = $200.

questions.title: Computing the Harberger Deadweight Loss Triangle
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a single-price monopolist faces linear inverse demand P = 150 - 3Q (so MR = 150 - 6Q) and constant Marginal Cost MC = $30 (with zero fixed cost). What is the Deadweight Loss (DWL) created by the monopoly relative to perfect competition?

hints.text: Solve for both the monopoly outcome (Q_M, P_M) using MR = MC and the competitive output Q_C using P = MC.
Apply the Harberger triangle formula: DWL = (1/2) * (Q_C - Q_M) * (P_M - MC).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Triangle Factor): Computing (Q_C - Q_M) * (P_M - MC) = (40 - 20) * ($90 - $30) = $1,200 calculates a rectangle (equal to monopoly profit) instead of the DWL triangle.
Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Price Height Error): Using P_M = $90 instead of the markup (P_M - MC) = $60 as the triangle height yields (1/2)(20)($90) = $900, overstating DWL by failing to subtract MC.
Diagnostic fallacy (Total Competitive Surplus Confusion): $2,400 = (1/2)(40)($150 - $30) is total social surplus under perfect competition (CS_C), not the portion lost to monopoly.

questions.title: Total Consumer Surplus Lost Under Single-Price Monopoly
questions.prompt_template: A market has inverse demand P = 80 - 2Q (so MR = 80 - 4Q) and constant MC = ATC = $16. By how much does Consumer Surplus decrease when the market is served by a single-price monopolist instead of a perfectly competitive industry (CS_C - CS_M)?

hints.text: Compute Consumer Surplus under perfect competition (P_C = $16, Q_C) and under single-price monopoly (P_M, Q_M), then take their difference.
Double-check your answer with surplus conservation: the drop in Consumer Surplus (CS_C - CS_M) must equal Monopoly Profit plus Deadweight Loss.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Remaining CS vs. Lost CS): $256 = (1/2)(16)($80 - $48) is the Consumer Surplus remaining under monopoly (and also equals DWL), not the total drop in CS.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted DWL From Consumer Loss): $512 = ($48 - $16) * 16 captures only the surplus transferred to monopoly profit and omits the additional $256 lost as Deadweight Loss.

Correct. Under competition, Q_C = 32 and CS_C = (1/2)(32)($80 - $16) = $1,024. Under monopoly, Q_M = 16, P_M = $48, and CS_M = (1/2)(16)($80 - $48) = $256. Consumer Surplus falls by $1,024 - $256 = $768 (= $512 profit + $256 DWL).
Diagnostic fallacy (Assumed Zero Monopoly CS): $1,024 is total competitive Consumer Surplus; buyers still retain $256 of Consumer Surplus under single-price monopoly.

questions.title: Average Total Cost and Required Subsidy Under Marginal-Cost Pricing
questions.prompt_template: A municipal broadband utility is a natural monopoly with annual Fixed Cost FC = $600,000 and constant Marginal Cost MC = $20 per subscriber-year. If regulators mandate marginal-cost pricing (P = MC = $20) and the utility serves Q = 10,000 subscribers, what is its Average Total Cost (ATC) and what annual lump-sum taxpayer subsidy is needed for the utility to break even?

hints.text: Calculate ATC = (FC / Q) + MC at Q = 10,000 subscribers.
The required subsidy equals the utility's total economic loss: (ATC - P) * Q.

options_template.text: ATC = $80 per subscriber; required subsidy = $600,000
options_template.feedback: Correct. At Q = 10,000, ATC = ($600,000 / 10,000) + $20 = $60 + $20 = $80. Charging P = $20 creates a loss of ($80 - $20) * 10,000 = $600,000, requiring a $600,000 subsidy to cover the uncovered fixed cost.

options_template.text: ATC = $60 per subscriber; required subsidy = $600,000
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (AFC-ATC Conflation): $600,000 / 10,000 = $60 is only Average Fixed Cost (AFC); you must add Average Variable Cost ($20) to get ATC = $80.

options_template.text: ATC = $80 per subscriber; required subsidy = $800,000
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Cost vs. Net Loss Error): $800,000 is Total Cost ($600,000 + $200,000), ignoring the $200,000 in subscriber revenue ($20 * 10,000) that already covers variable costs.

options_template.text: ATC = $80 per subscriber; required subsidy = $200,000
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Loss Swap): $200,000 = $20 * 10,000 is the utility's subscriber revenue (and total variable cost), not its economic loss.

questions.title: Solving Monopoly and Competitive Equilibria With Upward-Sloping MC
questions.prompt_template: A single-price monopolist faces inverse demand P = 100 - Q (so MR = 100 - 2Q) and an upward-sloping Marginal Cost curve MC = 10 + Q. What are the monopoly quantity (Q_M), monopoly price (P_M), and competitive benchmark quantity (Q_C)?

hints.text: Equate MR = MC to solve for Q_M, substitute Q_M into Demand for P_M, and separately equate P = MC to find Q_C.
Be careful: the shortcut Q_C = 2 * Q_M holds only when Marginal Cost is constant—not when MC slopes upward.

options_template.text: Q_M = 30 units, P_M = $40, Q_C = 45 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR = MC Price-Reading Fallacy): $40 is the value of MR and MC at Q_M = 30 (10 + 30 = $40); plugging Q_M = 30 into Demand gives P_M = 100 - 30 = $70.

options_template.text: Q_M = 30 units, P_M = $70, Q_C = 60 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overgeneralized Constant-MC Shortcut): Doubling Q_M to get Q_C = 60 fails when MC slopes upward; setting 100 - Q_C = 10 + Q_C yields 2Q_C = 90, so Q_C = 45.

options_template.text: Q_M = 45 units, P_M = $55, Q_C = 45 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Rule Applied to Monopoly): Setting P = MC (100 - Q = 10 + Q) gives the competitive outcome (45, $55) instead of equating MR = MC for the monopolist.

options_template.text: Q_M = 30 units, P_M = $70, Q_C = 45 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting MR = MC gives 100 - 2Q_M = 10 + Q_M -> 3Q_M = 90 -> Q_M = 30 and P_M = 100 - 30 = $70. Setting P = MC gives 100 - Q_C = 10 + Q_C -> 2Q_C = 90 -> Q_C = 45.

questions.title: Output and Profit Under Perfect Price Discrimination
questions.prompt_template: A monopolist faces linear inverse demand P = 90 - 3Q and constant Marginal Cost MC = $18 (with zero fixed cost). If the firm practices first-degree (perfect) price discrimination—charging every buyer their exact maximum willingness to pay—what output (Q*) does it produce and what economic profit does it earn?

hints.text: Under perfect price discrimination, MR = P, so the firm produces every unit for which buyer willingness to pay is at least MC ($18).
Economic profit equals the entire surplus triangle between the demand curve and MC from Q = 0 to Q*.

options_template.text: Q* = 12 units, economic profit = $432
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Price Monopoly Solution): Q = 12 and profit = $432 are the single-price monopoly outcomes (where MR = 90 - 6Q = 18); perfect price discrimination doubles output to Q* = 24 and captures the full $864 surplus.

options_template.text: Q* = 24 units, economic profit = $864
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting P = MC gives 90 - 3Q* = 18 -> 3Q* = 72 -> Q* = 24 units. Profit equals the entire surplus triangle: (1/2) * ($90 - $18) * 24 = (1/2)($72)(24) = $864.

options_template.text: Q* = 24 units, economic profit = $1,296
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reported Total Revenue Instead of Profit): $1,296 is Total Revenue ($864 triangle + $432 variable cost rectangle) before subtracting Total Cost ($18 * 24 = $432).

options_template.text: Q* = 24 units, economic profit = $1,728
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Triangle Factor): Computing ($90 - $18) * 24 = $1,728 assumes every single buyer pays the $90 choke price rather than moving down the demand curve.

questions.title: Optimal Segmented Prices and Profit for a Museum
questions.prompt_template: A museum with constant Marginal Cost MC = $6 per visitor (zero fixed cost) prevents ticket resale and segments visitors into two linear demand groups: Tourists with P_1 = 46 - 2Q_1 (MR_1 = 46 - 4Q_1) and Local Residents with P_2 = 22 - Q_2 (MR_2 = 22 - 2Q_2). Under third-degree price discrimination, what profit-maximizing prices (P_1*, P_2*) should it charge and what is its combined economic profit?

hints.text: Equate MR_1 = $6 and MR_2 = $6 separately to find Q_1* and Q_2*, then plug each quantity into its own inverse demand curve.
Add the two segment profits: pi_1 = (P_1* - 6) * Q_1* and pi_2 = (P_2* - 6) * Q_2*.

options_template.text: P_1* = $26, P_2* = $14, combined profit = $372
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Combined Revenue vs. Profit): $372 = ($26 * 10) + ($14 * 8) is combined Total Revenue before subtracting Total Cost ($6 * 18 = $108).

options_template.text: P_1* = $26, P_2* = $14, combined profit = $132
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Triangle Formula Applied to Profit Boxes): Profit in each segment is a rectangle (P_i* - MC) * Q_i*, not a triangle; multiplying by 1/2 erroneously halves combined profit from $264 to $132.

options_template.text: P_1* = $26, P_2* = $14, combined profit = $264
P_1* = $20, P_2* = $20, combined profit = $210
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform Averaging Heuristic): Charging the simple midpoint price of $20 to both groups eliminates price discrimination and reduces profit to ($20 - $6)(13 + 2) = $210.

questions.title: Computing the Lerner Index and Optimal Price From Elasticity
questions.prompt_template: A profit-maximizing monopolist operates with constant Marginal Cost MC = $30. At its optimal output, the point price elasticity of demand is |e_d| = 2.5. Using the inverse-elasticity rule, what are the monopolist's Lerner Index (L) and profit-maximizing price (P_M)?

hints.text: First compute the Lerner Index L = 1 / |e_d| = (P_M - MC) / P_M.
Rearrange (P_M - MC) / P_M = L into P_M * (1 - L) = MC, then solve for P_M = MC / (1 - L).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Plus Markup Confusion): Multiplying $30 * 1.40 = $42 treats 0.40 as a markup over MC rather than a margin over P_M; at P = $42, (42 - 30)/42 is only 0.286, not 0.40.
Diagnostic fallacy (Complement-of-L Error): 0.60 equals (1 - 1/|e_d|), not L; mistakenly setting L = 0.60 yields P = 30 / 0.40 = $75.
Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Price Substitution): Charging P_M = MC = $30 would produce a Lerner Index of 0, contradicting L = 0.40.

questions.topic: Price Discrimination vs. Uniform Pricing Profit
questions.title: Profit Gain From Third-Degree Price Discrimination Over Uniform Pricing
questions.prompt_template: A software vendor has constant MC = $10 per license (zero fixed cost) and serves two separated segments: Business Users with P_1 = 70 - 2Q_1 (Q_1 = 35 - 0.5P) and Students with P_2 = 40 - Q_2 (Q_2 = 40 - P). For uniform prices P <= $40, combined demand is Q = 75 - 1.5P (inverse demand P = 50 - (2/3)Q, MR = 50 - (4/3)Q). How much ADDITIONAL economic profit does the vendor earn under third-degree price discrimination compared to charging the profit-maximizing uniform price to both segments?

hints.text: Compute combined profit under third-degree price discrimination (equating MR_1 = 10 and MR_2 = 10 separately), then compute profit under the optimal uniform price (equating combined MR = 10).
Take the difference: Profit Gain = pi_PD - pi_Uniform.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Profit vs. Profit Gain): $675 ($450 from business + $225 from students) is the total profit under price discrimination, not the additional gain over uniform pricing ($600).

Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Benchmark Comparison): $225 compares price discrimination ($675) against serving business users alone ($450) rather than the higher-profit uniform price ($30, yielding $600) that serves both groups.

Diagnostic fallacy (Same-Output Zero-Gain Fallacy): Even though combined output happens to remain 30 licenses in both regimes, reallocating licenses from a uniform $30 price to $40 (business) and $25 (students) raises profit by $75.

Correct. Under price discrimination, Q_1* = 15 (P_1* = $40, pi_1 = $450) and Q_2* = 15 (P_2* = $25, pi_2 = $225), totaling $675. Under uniform pricing, 50 - (4/3)Q = 10 gives Q_SP = 30 and P_SP = $30, yielding ($30 - $10)(30) = $600. The profit gain is $675 - $600 = +$75.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Weighing Static Deadweight Loss Against Dynamic R&D Incentives
questions.prompt_template: If single-price monopoly creates higher prices and deadweight loss, why do U.S. policymakers deliberately grant biotech firms a temporary 20-year utility patent on newly developed breakthrough therapies?

hints.text: Consider the dynamic trade-off between static efficiency today and the incentive to fund risky research and development upfront.
Ask whether a biotech firm would invest heavily in discovering a new therapy if competitors could immediately copy the formula at marginal production cost.

options_template.text: Because patents guarantee that pharmaceutical marginal cost drops to zero immediately after approval.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Reduction Myth): Patents are legal barriers to entry that protect pricing power; they do not automatically eliminate manufacturing marginal costs.

options_template.text: To accept temporary static deadweight loss during the patent window in exchange for incentivizing risky, high-fixed-cost R&D that might not occur if rivals could copy the formula immediately.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Patent policy reflects a deliberate economic trade-off: temporary monopoly profits reward upfront innovation, after which patent expiration allows generic competition to expand output and cut prices.

options_template.text: Because pharmaceutical manufacturing is always a natural monopoly requiring a permanent government franchise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Natural vs. Legal Monopoly Conflation): Once a drug formula is known, multiple generic manufacturers can produce it efficiently; pharmaceutical monopolies are legal (patent-based), not permanent natural monopolies.

options_template.text: Because temporary monopolies completely eliminate Deadweight Loss while maximizing Consumer Surplus during the patent term.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Welfare Contradiction): During the patent window, single-price monopoly pricing still creates Deadweight Loss and reduces short-run Consumer Surplus; the justification is dynamic innovation, not static zero DWL.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Breaking Up a Natural Monopoly Can Raise Costs
questions.prompt_template: A city council proposes breaking up its single regional electric distribution grid into four competing utility companies, each building its own separate network of neighborhood power lines. Based on natural monopoly theory, what is the primary economic flaw in this proposal?

hints.text: Think about where each of the four smaller utilities would sit on the declining Long-Run Average Total Cost (LRATC) curve.
Splitting fixed infrastructure across four duplicate networks reduces each firm's customer volume.

options_template.text: Duplicating massive fixed infrastructure forces each smaller utility up onto a higher point on the declining LRATC curve, raising average cost per household.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because a natural monopoly exhibits continuous economies of scale across market demand, splitting one network into four duplicate grids wastes fixed capital and increases average total cost.

options_template.text: Four competing electric grids would immediately reduce fixed infrastructure spending to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Elimination Myth): Building four parallel sets of power lines quadruples fixed network infrastructure rather than eliminating it.

options_template.text: Breaking up the utility violates the Lerner Index because four firms always charge a higher price than an unregulated monopolist.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competition-Price Paradox): More competition puts downward pressure on markups, but the specific flaw in breaking up a natural monopoly is losing economies of scale (higher LRATC), not higher markups.

options_template.text: Electricity demand becomes perfectly elastic only when served by a single unregulated seller.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity-Structure Inversion): Market demand elasticity depends on consumer preferences and substitutes, not on the number of sellers; a single seller faces downward-sloping market demand, not perfectly elastic demand.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating Marginal-Cost vs. Average-Cost Utility Regulation
questions.prompt_template: A state public utility commission regulates a natural monopoly water provider whose LRATC declines continuously across market demand (so MC < LRATC). Why might regulators choose Average-Cost (fair-return) pricing (P = ATC) instead of Marginal-Cost pricing (P = MC)?

hints.text: Compare the utility's economic profit and fiscal impact on taxpayers under P = MC versus P = ATC.
Remember that P = MC eliminates DWL but creates an ongoing operating loss whenever MC < ATC.

options_template.text: Because Average-Cost pricing completely eliminates Deadweight Loss while guaranteeing large economic profits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Efficiency-Profit Double Error): Fair-return pricing (P = ATC) yields zero economic profit—not large profits—and leaves a small residual Deadweight Loss since P = ATC > MC.

options_template.text: Because Marginal-Cost pricing forces the utility to produce less output than an unregulated monopolist.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output Comparison Reversal): Marginal-cost pricing expands output to the largest, allocatively efficient quantity (Q_C), well above the unregulated monopoly output Q_M.

options_template.text: Because Average-Cost pricing lets the utility break even without an ongoing taxpayer subsidy, while still lowering price and shrinking Deadweight Loss relative to unregulated monopoly.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under P = MC, the natural monopolist loses money because MC < ATC and requires public subsidies; fair-return pricing (P = ATC) avoids subsidies while capturing most of the efficiency gains over unregulated monopoly.

options_template.text: Because Average-Cost pricing causes the utility's marginal cost to rise above its average total cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Induced Cost Distortion): Regulating the price charged to customers does not change the underlying engineering relationship where MC < LRATC.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Solving the Natural Monopoly Pricing Dilemma With a Two-Part Tariff
questions.prompt_template: Recall the regional hospital MRI scanner with $900,000 in annual fixed equipment and staffing costs and a constant $100 marginal cost per scan. How can a regional health network use a two-part tariff (a fixed annual access fee paid by insurers/members plus a $100 per-scan usage fee) to overcome the classic natural monopoly regulation dilemma?

hints.text: Separate the goal of covering the $900,000 fixed cost from the goal of encouraging every medically valuable scan whose benefit exceeds $100.
Ask which part of the two-part tariff covers fixed costs and which part preserves allocative efficiency at the margin.

options_template.text: By raising the per-scan fee above $400 so fewer patients use the scanner, reducing fixed equipment costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Reduction Illusion): Cutting scan volume does not reduce the $900,000 fixed cost; it raises ATC per scan and increases Deadweight Loss from forgone scans.

options_template.text: By eliminating the $100 marginal cost of each scan so the hospital can offer unlimited free imaging.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Elimination Myth): Pricing schemes change how costs are financed, not the real $100 marginal resource cost of performing a scan.

options_template.text: By setting the per-scan fee equal to zero and relying on unregulated monopoly markups to eliminate Deadweight Loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Price Overuse & Markup Contradiction): A $0 per-scan fee encourages overuse where MB < $100, and unregulated monopoly markups create—not eliminate—Deadweight Loss.

options_template.text: By using the fixed access fee to cover the $900,000 fixed cost while pricing each individual scan at MC = $100 so no scan valued above $100 goes unperformed.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A two-part tariff decouples fixed-cost recovery (via the fixed access fee) from marginal pricing (P = MC = $100), allowing the hospital to break even without creating per-scan deadweight loss.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: When Third-Degree Price Discrimination Improves Social Welfare
questions.prompt_template: A campus theater currently charges a single uniform ticket price so high that low-income students buy zero tickets. If the theater introduces verified student discounts while raising general-public ticket prices slightly, under what condition can this third-degree price discrimination reduce total Deadweight Loss?

hints.text: Recall that Deadweight Loss shrinks when mutually beneficial trades (where buyer WTP > MC) increase overall.
Focus on what happens to total tickets sold when a previously priced-out elastic segment enters the market.

options_template.text: Only if the theater raises prices on students above the general-public price to discourage attendance.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Segmentation Error): Students are the more elastic segment; raising their price would keep them priced out and reduce output rather than expand it.

options_template.text: When the discounted student price brings previously priced-out buyers into the market so that total combined output expands toward the competitive level.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Whenever third-degree price discrimination expands total output by serving more elastic buyers who were excluded under uniform pricing, previously lost trades occur and Deadweight Loss can fall.

options_template.text: Whenever the theater's total profit increases, because higher monopoly profit always implies lower Deadweight Loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profit-Welfare Equivalence Myth): Price discrimination always raises firm profit, but if total output does not increase (or falls), Deadweight Loss can actually stay the same or rise.

options_template.text: Never—third-degree price discrimination always increases Deadweight Loss and harms every consumer group.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Universal-Harm Myth): More elastic buyers (like students) directly benefit from lower discounted prices, and opening previously unserved markets reduces Deadweight Loss.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Impact of Arbitrage on Software Academic Licensing
questions.prompt_template: A software company sells commercial licenses to corporations at $600 per year and academic licenses to verified students at $120 per year. Suppose the company removes `.edu` account verification and allows license keys to be transferred freely on online resale marketplaces. What is the predicted market outcome?

hints.text: Identify which of the three necessary conditions for price discrimination has just broken down.
Ask what enterprising buyers will do when the exact same license can be bought for $120 and resold to firms willing to pay up to $600.

options_template.text: Corporations will continue paying $600 willingly, and the software vendor's profits will double.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Arbitrage Incentives): Rational corporate buyers will not pay $600 directly when identical transferable keys are available on the resale market for far less.

options_template.text: Student demand will become perfectly inelastic, allowing the company to raise student prices above $600.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity-Reversal Error): Allowing resale does not make students less price-sensitive; it merges the two segments into a single resale-connected market.

options_template.text: Arbitrage will undermine market segmentation as low-price buyers resell keys to corporations, forcing the vendor back toward a single uniform price and lower profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Preventing arbitrage is essential for price discrimination; unrestricted resale lets $120 buyers undercut the $600 corporate tier, collapsing the dual-price structure and reducing vendor profit.

options_template.text: The software vendor will automatically transition to first-degree (perfect) price discrimination.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (First-Degree Misclassification): Perfect price discrimination requires strict prevention of resale plus individualized pricing—the exact opposite of an open resale market.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Economic Rationale Behind Airline Advance-Purchase and Stay Restrictions
questions.prompt_template: Why do airlines charge significantly higher fares for last-minute, flexible weekday tickets than for non-refundable tickets booked weeks in advance with a Saturday-night stay, even when both passengers sit in identical economy seats on the same aircraft?

hints.text: First check whether serving the two passengers costs the airline dramatically different marginal costs, then examine their price elasticities of demand.
Time-sensitive business travelers have less elastic demand than flexible leisure travelers.
