options_template.text: To segment less elastic business travelers from more elastic leisure travelers via self-selection and charge a higher markup to the less elastic segment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since flying both passengers in identical seats involves nearly identical marginal cost, advance-purchase and weekend-stay hurdles separate price-insensitive business flyers from flexible leisure flyers so the airline can price-discriminate.

options_template.text: Because carrying a business traveler uses significantly more jet fuel per seat than carrying a leisure traveler.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Justification Myth): Price discrimination specifically refers to price differences NOT justified by cost differences; seat marginal costs on the same flight are virtually identical.

options_template.text: Because airlines are perfectly competitive price takers forced by regulators to subsidize weekend trips.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Taker Misclassification): Perfect competitors cannot charge different prices for identical seats; airline fare classes depend on market power and non-transferable tickets.

options_template.text: Because business travelers have more elastic demand than leisure travelers and therefore accept higher prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity-Markup Reversal): Buyers with MORE elastic demand are more price-sensitive and receive lower prices; business travelers pay higher fares precisely because their demand is LESS elastic.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Price Ceilings Under Monopoly vs. Competition
questions.title: Contrasting a Binding Price Ceiling in Monopoly vs. Perfect Competition
questions.prompt_template: In a perfectly competitive market, a binding price ceiling set below equilibrium creates a shortage and Deadweight Loss. Now consider a single-price monopolist with constant MC = $20 whose unregulated equilibrium is Q_M = 20 and P_M = $60 (while competitive output is Q_C = 40). If regulators impose a price ceiling at P_bar = $20 (equal to MC), what happens to the monopolist's output and Deadweight Loss?

hints.text: Think about the monopolist's Marginal Revenue for every unit up to Q = 40 when the maximum legal price is fixed at $20.
When the ceiling caps price at $20, selling an extra unit no longer lowers the price on prior units—so MR = $20 all the way up to Q = 40.

options_template.text: The monopolist cuts output below 20 units, creating a severe shortage and doubling Deadweight Loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive-Ceiling Transfer): Unlike a competitive industry with an upward-sloping supply curve, a monopolist facing a ceiling at P = MC sees its negative price effect vanish up to Q_C, giving it an incentive to expand output.

options_template.text: Output stays frozen at Q_M = 20 because a monopolist never responds to regulated prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frozen-MR Assumption): A binding price ceiling makes the effective demand and MR curves horizontal at $20 up to Q = 40, shifting the firm's optimal output rightward.

options_template.text: The monopolist expands output to Q = 50 (the choke quantity), creating overproduction Deadweight Loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Excess-Output Error): Beyond Q = 40, buyer willingness to pay drops below $20 = MC, so the firm will not sell units past Q = 40.

options_template.text: Output expands from 20 to 40 units and Deadweight Loss falls to zero because the ceiling removes the monopolist's ability to raise price by restricting output.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Capping price at P = MC = $20 makes effective MR = $20 up to Q_C = 40, eliminating the price effect of expanding sales; output rises from 20 to 40 and Deadweight Loss vanishes (assuming ATC <= $20).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing High Markups Alongside Negative Economic Profit
questions.prompt_template: A biotech firm holds a monopoly patent on a rare-disease therapy. Its marginal manufacturing cost is $40 per dose, its profit-maximizing monopoly price is $200 per dose (yielding a Lerner Index of 0.80), yet its annual financial audit shows a negative economic profit. How is this combination economically possible?

hints.text: Distinguish between the firm's per-unit markup over Marginal Cost (P_M - MC) and its total profit net of Fixed Costs (P_M - ATC).
Consider how massive upfront R&D and clinical-trial fixed costs affect ATC when patient volume for a rare disease is very small.

options_template.text: It is mathematically impossible; any firm with P_M > MC must earn positive economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MC-ATC Conflation): Positive contribution margin (P_M > MC) covers variable costs, but total profit is positive only if P_M also exceeds Average Total Cost (ATC).

options_template.text: High upfront fixed R&D costs spread over a small rare-disease patient population push ATC above $200 per dose, so P_M > MC yet P_M < ATC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A high Lerner Index measures markup over marginal cost, not overall profitability; massive fixed R&D costs divided by low unit volume can easily leave ATC > P_M and produce an economic loss.

options_template.text: The firm must be operating on the inelastic portion of demand where raising the price lowers profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic-Range Misdiagnosis): A Lerner Index of 0.80 corresponds to |e_d| = 1 / 0.80 = 1.25 > 1, confirming the firm is already in the elastic region.

options_template.text: The firm should lower its price to $40 (MC) to eliminate its economic loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive-Pricing Rescue Myth): Lowering price to MC = $40 would cut contribution margin to zero and increase the economic loss to 100% of fixed costs.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Superior Technology Alone May Not Displace a Network Monopolist
questions.prompt_template: A startup launches a peer-to-peer payment app with lower per-transaction marginal costs and a cleaner interface than the dominant incumbent app used by almost everyone in the region. Despite offering lower fees, the startup struggles to gain active users. Which Chapter 8 concept best explains this persistence of monopoly power?

hints.text: Ask why a consumer might stay with the incumbent payment app even if the new app has slightly lower fees.
Remember the four primary barriers to entry: resource control, legal franchises, network effects, and natural monopoly.

options_template.text: Exclusive control of a scarce physical natural resource required to build mobile apps.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Resource-Barrier Misattribution): Payment apps rely on widely available software and servers, not exclusive ownership of a scarce mineral or physical input.

options_template.text: First-degree price discrimination preventing the startup from writing software code.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pricing-Entry Conflation): First-degree price discrimination describes extracting individual buyer willingness to pay, not why users hesitate to leave a large payment network.

options_template.text: Strong network effects: because a payment app's value depends on how many counterparties already use it, a small entrant faces a steep barrier to attracting users away from the incumbent.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under strong network effects, users value being on the same platform as their friends and merchants, allowing an established incumbent to retain dominance even against a lower-cost entrant.

options_template.text: Perfectly competitive zero-profit equilibrium preventing either firm from advertising.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive-Model Misapplication): A dominant incumbent shielding market share against entry is a classic barrier-to-entry phenomenon, not perfect competition.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Efficiency vs. Equity Under Perfect Price Discrimination
questions.title: Reconciling Allocative Efficiency With Zero Consumer Surplus
questions.prompt_template: A policymaker argues that first-degree (perfect) price discrimination is 'just as socially efficient as perfect competition, so consumers should be equally happy with both market outcomes.' How should an economist evaluate this claim?

hints.text: Separate allocative efficiency (size of the total surplus pie and DWL) from distributional equity (who gets the slices of that pie).
Compare total output Q, Deadweight Loss, and Consumer Surplus across Perfect Competition and Perfect Price Discrimination.

options_template.text: The efficiency claim is right—both produce Q_C with zero Deadweight Loss—but the consumer-welfare conclusion is wrong because perfect price discrimination transfers 100% of Consumer Surplus to the monopolist (CS = $0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Perfect price discrimination achieves allocative efficiency (Q = Q_C, DWL = $0), yet it creates an extreme distributional shift: consumers retain zero surplus while the firm captures the entire social surplus.

options_template.text: Both parts of the claim are completely right because zero Deadweight Loss guarantees that Consumer Surplus is maximized.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Efficiency-Equity Conflation): Zero Deadweight Loss means total surplus (CS + PS) is maximized, NOT that Consumer Surplus is maximized; here CS = $0.

options_template.text: Both parts of the claim are wrong because perfect price discrimination restricts output below Q_M and maximizes Deadweight Loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output-Direction Error): Perfect price discrimination expands output all the way to Q_C and eliminates Deadweight Loss.

options_template.text: The consumer-welfare conclusion is right, but perfect price discrimination is inefficient because it eliminates all producer profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Recipient Inversion): Perfect price discrimination maximizes—rather than eliminates—producer profit while eliminating Consumer Surplus.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Critiquing an Executive Claim About Operating in the Inelastic Region
questions.prompt_template: The pricing director of a regional monopoly tells the board: 'At our current price, our estimated price elasticity of demand is |e_d| = 0.6. Since demand is inelastic, customers barely cut back when we hold prices low—let's expand sales further at an even lower price to lock in volume.' Using Chapter 8 principles, what is the strongest economic critique of this advice?

hints.text: Evaluate Marginal Revenue when |e_d| = 0.6 < 1 using the Amoroso-Robinson relation MR = P * (1 - 1/|e_d|).
If MR is negative at the current output, ask whether the firm should lower price (expand Q) or raise price (restrict Q).

options_template.text: The director is right: cutting price in the inelastic region increases both total revenue and total profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic Revenue-Direction Error): When |e_d| < 1, lowering price causes a smaller percentage gain in quantity than the percentage drop in price, so total revenue falls while total cost rises.

options_template.text: The firm should keep price unchanged because |e_d| = 0.6 maximizes total revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (TR-Max Elasticity Error): Total revenue is maximized at unit elasticity (|e_d| = 1, where MR = 0), not at |e_d| = 0.6.

options_template.text: The firm should expand output until |e_d| reaches 0, where the Lerner Index equals 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Elasticity Optimum Error): As |e_d| approaches 0, MR becomes more deeply negative; profit maximization with MC >= 0 requires |e_d| > 1.

options_template.text: Because |e_d| = 0.6 < 1 implies MR < 0, cutting price to expand volume will LOWER total revenue while RAISING total cost; the firm should instead RAISE price and reduce output until it reaches the elastic region (|e_d| > 1) where MR = MC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At |e_d| = 0.6, MR = P(1 - 1/0.6) = -(2/3)P < 0. Raising price (cutting output) simultaneously increases total revenue and reduces total cost, strictly raising profit until MR = MC >= 0 in the elastic range.
